--- title: "Data Wrangling" subtitle: "Introduction to Global Health Data Science" date: "2026-09-14" format: revealjs: output-file: w04-l01-wrangling-slides.html footer: "[🔗 sta198-fa26-2.github.io](https://sta198-fa26-2.github.io/)" theme: slides.scss transition: fade slide-number: true pdf-separate-fragments: true toc: false html: code-link: true filters: - ../remove-fmt-skip.lua editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ## Main Ideas - Organizing our data according to a consistent set of "tidy" principles makes data easy to work with and leverages the ways `R` is effective. - Often we need to wrangle our data in order to extract meaning (including creating new variables, calculating summary statistics, subsetting data, etc). - Using only **seven key verbs** we can accomplish a wide variety of data wrangling tasks. ## Tidy Principles Tidy data have three related characteristics 1. Each variable forms a column. 2. Each observation forms a row. 3. Each value has its own cell. ## Rural and Urban Patterns of Global Obesity
Obesity is a major risk factor for numerous non-communicable diseases, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, stroke, and some cancers. We consider data from an exercise developed by the [Johns Hopkins Open Case Studies Project](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bp-rural-and-urban-obesity/#Motivation) on average body mass index around the world.
Body mass index (BMI) is calculated as weight in kg divided by the square of height in m: $BMI=\frac{kg}{m^2}$. While it is not a perfect surrogate for say visceral fat (e.g., people may have a high BMI due to muscle mass rather than visceral fat), it is an easily-obtained surrogate that is often used in large studies of health. The World Health Organization acknowledges that while BMI is a useful indicator at the population level, it is only a rough guide at the individual level because it does not always correspond to the same body fat % in different individuals.
## WHO Classification of BMI ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../img/whobmi.jpg){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Data Our data include summaries of BMI from 200 countries worldwide, both at the national level and in urban and rural areas separately, for the years 1985 and 2017, separately for men and women. The original data source is NCD-RisC, the non-communicable disease risk factor collaboration. 2017 remains the most recent year for which they have published BMI broken out by urban/rural status. ## Data Wrangling
Often we need to wrangle our data to extract meaning. This includes calculating new variables, summary statistics, grouping by variables, renaming, reordering, selecting subsets of data, filtering by various conditions, etc. We can accomplish a great deal of wrangling by learning just **seven key verbs**. Each of these functions takes a data frame as input and returns a data frame as output. - filter - arrange - select - slice - mutate - summarize - group_by
--- We first explore the data a bit. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} load("../data/BMI_long.Rdata") glimpse(BMI_long) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 2,400 Columns: 5 $ Country "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", "A… $ Sex "Men", "Men", "Men", "Men", "Men", "Men", "Wome… $ Region "National", "Rural", "Urban", "National", "Rura… $ Year "1985", "1985", "1985", "2017", "2017", "2017",… $ BMI 20.2, 19.7, 22.4, 22.8, 22.5, 23.6, 20.6, 20.1,… ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} names(BMI_long) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Country" "Sex" "Region" "Year" "BMI" ``` ::: ::: --- ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(BMI_long) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Afghanistan Men National 1985 20.2 2 Afghanistan Men Rural 1985 19.7 3 Afghanistan Men Urban 1985 22.4 4 Afghanistan Men National 2017 22.8 5 Afghanistan Men Rural 2017 22.5 6 Afghanistan Men Urban 2017 23.6 ``` ::: ::: The `head()` function returns "A tibble: 6 x 5" and then the first six rows of the `BMI_long` data. A **tibble** is a tweaked, opinionated version of the `R` data frame. --- There are a few differences a `tidyverse` tibble and an `R` data frame. We discuss two primary differences. First, a tibble provides more information than a data frame. When you print a tibble, it will show the first ten rows and all of the columns that fit on the screen, along with the type of each column. You can modify the number of rows and columns shown using the `print()` function options. Second, tibbles are somewhat more strict than data frames when it comes to subsetting data. --- ### `select()` The `select()` function picks off one or more columns by name. Let's say we want a dataset that only contains the variable BMI. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} select(BMI_long, BMI) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 1 BMI 1 20.2 2 19.7 3 22.4 4 22.8 5 22.5 6 23.6 # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- We can also use `select()` to exclude variables. Let's exclude `BMI` but keep all other variables. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} select(BMI_long, -BMI) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 4 Country Sex Region Year 1 Afghanistan Men National 1985 2 Afghanistan Men Rural 1985 3 Afghanistan Men Urban 1985 4 Afghanistan Men National 2017 5 Afghanistan Men Rural 2017 6 Afghanistan Men Urban 2017 # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- We can also use `select()` to select a range of variables. Here, we select the first three variables. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} select(BMI_long, Country:Region) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 3 Country Sex Region 1 Afghanistan Men National 2 Afghanistan Men Rural 3 Afghanistan Men Urban 4 Afghanistan Men National 5 Afghanistan Men Rural 6 Afghanistan Men Urban # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- ### `arrange()` The `arrange()` function orders rows (observations) in specific ways. Let's arrange the data by descending BMI, with large BMI values on top. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange(BMI_long, desc(BMI)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 American Samoa Women Urban 2017 35.4 2 American Samoa Women National 2017 35.3 3 American Samoa Women Rural 2017 35 4 Samoa Women Urban 2017 34.7 5 American Samoa Men Rural 2017 34.6 6 American Samoa Women Urban 1985 34.4 # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- Or with low BMI values on top. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange(BMI_long, BMI) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Bangladesh Women Rural 1985 17.7 2 Bangladesh Women National 1985 18.2 3 Timor-Leste Women Rural 1985 18.2 4 Viet Nam Women Rural 1985 18.2 5 Nepal Women Rural 1985 18.3 6 Ethiopia Men Rural 1985 18.4 # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- Or by two factors... ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange(BMI_long, desc(Country), BMI) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Zimbabwe Men Rural 1985 20.9 2 Zimbabwe Men National 1985 21.2 3 Zimbabwe Men Rural 2017 21.9 4 Zimbabwe Men Urban 1985 22.1 5 Zimbabwe Men National 2017 22.3 6 Zimbabwe Men Urban 2017 23.3 # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- ### The Pipe The pipe is a technique for passing information from one process to another. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% arrange(desc(BMI)) %>% select(Country, BMI) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 2 Country BMI 1 American Samoa 35.4 2 American Samoa 35.3 3 American Samoa 35 4 Samoa 34.7 5 American Samoa 34.6 6 American Samoa 34.4 # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: When reading code "in English", say "and then" whenever you see a pipe. --- R also has an alternative pipe, which is `|>` instead of `%>%`. Feel free to use either one. Keyboard shortcut: command-shift-M (mac) or control-shift-M (windows) --- ### `slice()` Slice selects rows based on their position. Here we slice off the first 5 rows of the `BMI_long` data. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% slice(1:5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Afghanistan Men National 1985 20.2 2 Afghanistan Men Rural 1985 19.7 3 Afghanistan Men Urban 1985 22.4 4 Afghanistan Men National 2017 22.8 5 Afghanistan Men Rural 2017 22.5 ``` ::: ::: --- **Question:** What is the code chunk below accomplishing? Guess before running the code. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% arrange(desc(BMI)) %>% slice(1:5) ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 American Samoa Women Urban 2017 35.4 2 American Samoa Women National 2017 35.3 3 American Samoa Women Rural 2017 35 4 Samoa Women Urban 2017 34.7 5 American Samoa Men Rural 2017 34.6 ``` ::: :::
--- To add comments to code, use the pound sign. This is helpful for debugging as well - you can temporarily disable a line. **Question:** What will happen if you comment out the line containing `arrange()` in the previous code chunk? Try it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% # arrange(desc(BMI)) %>% slice(1:5) ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Afghanistan Men National 1985 20.2 2 Afghanistan Men Rural 1985 19.7 3 Afghanistan Men Urban 1985 22.4 4 Afghanistan Men National 2017 22.8 5 Afghanistan Men Rural 2017 22.5 ``` ::: :::
--- ### `filter()` `filter()` selects rows satisfying certain conditions. We can use a single condition. Here we select all rows where the country is Iceland. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% filter(Country == "Iceland") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 12 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Iceland Men National 1985 24.8 2 Iceland Men Rural 1985 25.2 3 Iceland Men Urban 1985 24.8 4 Iceland Men National 2017 27.1 5 Iceland Men Rural 2017 27.3 6 Iceland Men Urban 2017 27.1 # ℹ 6 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- We can use more than one condition. Here we select all rows where the Country is Iceland and the year is 2017. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% filter(Country == "Iceland", Year == 2017) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Iceland Men National 2017 27.1 2 Iceland Men Rural 2017 27.3 3 Iceland Men Urban 2017 27.1 4 Iceland Women National 2017 25.5 5 Iceland Women Rural 2017 25.9 6 Iceland Women Urban 2017 25.5 ``` ::: ::: --- More complex conditions are possible! **Question:** In plain English, what is the code below accomplishing? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% filter(Country %in% c("Iceland", "Ireland"), Year == 2017 | Region == "National") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 16 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Iceland Men National 1985 24.8 2 Iceland Men National 2017 27.1 3 Iceland Men Rural 2017 27.3 4 Iceland Men Urban 2017 27.1 5 Iceland Women National 1985 24.3 6 Iceland Women National 2017 25.5 # ℹ 10 more rows ``` ::: ::: --- The table of logical operators below will be helpful as you work with filtering. |operator | definition | |:----------|:--------| | `<` | is less than? | | `<=` | is less than or equal to? | | `>` | is greater than? | | `>=` | is greater than or equal to? | | `==` | is exactly equal to? | | `!=` | is not equal to? | | `x & y` | is x AND y? | | `x` $\mid$ `y` | is x OR y? | --- The table of logical operators below will be helpful as you work with filtering. |operator | definition | |:----------|:--------| | `is.na(x)` | is x NA? | | `!is.na(x)` | is x not NA? | | `x %in% y` | is x in y? | | `!(x %in% y)` | is x not in y? | | `!x` | is not x? |
The final operator only makes sense if `x` is logical (TRUE / FALSE). R denotes missing values by NA. Missing values can cause biased or misleading results in any analysis, and it is important to understand why values are missing before drawing conclusions from data, especially if the fraction of missing values is not very small.
--- ### `mutate()` `mutate()` creates a new variable. Here we categorize BMI using the WHO classification. Here's our code: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut(BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c( "Underweight", "Normal Range", "Overweight", "Obese I", "Obese II", "Obese III" ), right = FALSE #intervals [a,b) )) %>% select(BMI, bmiclass) ``` ::: --- ### `mutate()` `mutate()` creates a new variable. Here we categorize BMI using the WHO classification. Here's our output: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 2 BMI bmiclass 1 20.2 Normal Range 2 19.7 Normal Range 3 22.4 Normal Range 4 22.8 Normal Range 5 22.5 Normal Range 6 23.6 Normal Range # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: ::: ---
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut( BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c( "Underweight", "Normal Range", "Overweight", "Obese I", "Obese II", "Obese III" ), right = FALSE )) %>% mutate(normal_range = bmiclass == "Normal Range") %>% print() ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2,400 × 7 Country Sex Region Year BMI bmiclass normal_range 1 Afghanistan Men National 1985 20.2 Normal Ran… TRUE 2 Afghanistan Men Rural 1985 19.7 Normal Ran… TRUE 3 Afghanistan Men Urban 1985 22.4 Normal Ran… TRUE 4 Afghanistan Men National 2017 22.8 Normal Ran… TRUE 5 Afghanistan Men Rural 2017 22.5 Normal Ran… TRUE 6 Afghanistan Men Urban 2017 23.6 Normal Ran… TRUE # ℹ 2,394 more rows ``` ::: :::
--- ### `summarize()`
`summarize` calculates summary statistics. It collapses rows into summary statistics and removes columns irrelevant to the calculation. Be sure to name your columns! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut(BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c( "Underweight", "Normal Range", "Overweight", "Obese I", "Obese II", "Obese III" ), right = FALSE )) %>% mutate(normal_range = bmiclass == "Normal Range") %>% summarize(fracnormal = mean(normal_range)) ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 fracnormal 1 NA ``` ::: :::
---
**Question:** The code chunk returns an NA. What is going wrong? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut(BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c( "Underweight", "Normal Range", "Overweight", "Obese I", "Obese II", "Obese III" ), right = FALSE )) %>% group_by(bmiclass) %>% count(bmiclass) %>% ungroup() ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 2 bmiclass n 1 Underweight 7 2 Normal Range 1185 3 Overweight 1091 4 Obese I 96 5 Obese II 3 6 18 ``` ::: ::: Ahh, count() is a very useful function!
---
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% count(BMI=="NA") ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 `BMI == "NA"` n 1 FALSE 2382 2 NA 18 ``` ::: ::: OK great, so the problem was with the source variable. We can just drop those few NA's when we take the mean, so that we get the mean of the observed values. In general, one would follow up on the NA values to understand why data were missing. What seems to be the issue here?
--- Let's print all 18 variables and see if we can tell what's going on. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% filter(is.na(BMI)==TRUE) %>% print(n=18) ``` ::: ## Investigating Missing Values ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 18 × 5 Country Sex Region Year BMI 1 Bermuda Men Rural 1985 NA 2 Bermuda Men Rural 2017 NA 3 Bermuda Women Rural 1985 NA 4 Bermuda Women Rural 2017 NA 5 China (Hong Kong SAR) Men Rural 2017 NA 6 China (Hong Kong SAR) Women Rural 2017 NA 7 Nauru Men Rural 1985 NA 8 Nauru Men Rural 2017 NA 9 Nauru Women Rural 1985 NA 10 Nauru Women Rural 2017 NA 11 Singapore Men Rural 1985 NA 12 Singapore Men Rural 2017 NA 13 Singapore Women Rural 1985 NA 14 Singapore Women Rural 2017 NA 15 Tokelau Men Urban 1985 NA 16 Tokelau Men Urban 2017 NA 17 Tokelau Women Urban 1985 NA 18 Tokelau Women Urban 2017 NA ``` ::: ::: This makes sense! Hong Kong, Singapore, Bermuda, and Nauru do not classify any of their population as rural; Tokelau does not classify any of its population as urban. ---
Finally, let's get the proportion of values with mean BMI in the normal range. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut(BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c( "Underweight", "Normal Range", "Overweight", "Obese I", "Obese II", "Obese III" ), right = FALSE )) %>% mutate(normal_range = bmiclass == "Normal Range") %>% summarize(fracnormal = mean(normal_range,na.rm=TRUE)) ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 fracnormal 1 0.497 ``` ::: :::
--- ### `group_by()`
`group_by()` is powerful when paired with summarize to calculate summary statistics by group. Here we find the proportion of means that are in the normal range for each region. If you don't `ungroup()` after you use it, there may be unforeseen consequences down the road, so this is good practice. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut(BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c("Underweight","Normal Range","Overweight","Obese I","Obese II","Obese III" ), right = FALSE )) %>% mutate(normal_range = bmiclass == "Normal Range") %>% group_by(Region) %>% summarize(fracnormal = mean(normal_range,na.rm=TRUE)) %>% ungroup() ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 Region fracnormal 1 National 0.506 2 Rural 0.541 3 Urban 0.446 ``` ::: :::
---
We can calculate more than one summary statistic in `summarize()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% mutate(bmiclass = cut( BMI, breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, 35, 40, Inf), labels = c( "Underweight", "Normal Range", "Overweight", "Obese I","Obese II","Obese III" ), right = FALSE )) %>% mutate(normal_range = bmiclass == "Normal Range") %>% group_by(Region) %>% summarize( fracnormal = mean(normal_range, na.rm = TRUE), max_BMI = max(BMI, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% ungroup() ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 Region fracnormal max_BMI 1 National 0.506 35.3 2 Rural 0.541 35 3 Urban 0.446 35.4 ``` ::: :::
---
**Question:** What is the code chunk below doing? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} BMI_long %>% count(Year) %>% mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) ``` :::
Click to reveal output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 3 Year n prop 1 1985 1200 0.5 2 2017 1200 0.5 ``` ::: :::
--- ### distinct()
One more nifty command is the `distinct` command in R, which eliminates duplicate rows. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age <- as_tibble(c(1,1,1,2,3)) age ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 1 value 1 1 2 1 3 1 4 2 5 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} distinct(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 1 value 1 1 2 2 3 3 ``` ::: :::
--- ### Additional Resources - [https://style.tidyverse.org/](https://style.tidyverse.org/) - [https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bp-rural-and-urban-obesity/](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bp-rural-and-urban-obesity/)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
